title: Mountain View CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Mountain View area wells have a 29 ft median depth and 12 gpm median yield. See what that means for drilling cost and water supply near Lakeside and Wheat Ridge.
h1: Understanding private wells around Mountain View, Colorado
intro_html:
In the Mountain View and Lakeside area, most wells are surprisingly shallow for the Front Range, and many produce solid household water. The state has over 11,000 well permits within about 5 miles here, so there’s a lot of history to learn from before you buy or build.

I’ll walk through how deep wells usually go, how much water they tend to make, what drilling costs look like in this part of the Denver Basin, and the main risks to check around Edgewater, Wheat Ridge and Berkley before you commit to a lot.

sections.heading: How deep wells run around Mountain View
sections.html:
Within about 5 miles of Mountain View, the median well depth on record is only 29 feet, and the middle half run 20–50 feet. That’s very shallow compared with a lot of Colorado mountain and basin wells. About 87% of wells are under 100 feet, and only 3% go deeper than 600 feet, even though the single deepest well hits 1,740 feet.

Most wells here are in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, with some alluvial influence along drainages. The shallow depths suggest driller bids will usually be based on shorter hole lengths, but that outlier depth tells you deep holes are possible if a particular spot is difficult. When you talk with a driller, use nearby well records as the starting point for a realistic depth range on your exact parcel.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water you can expect
sections.html:
Yields in the Mountain View area are generally favorable for household use. The median reported pump yield is 12.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 8.0 and 15.0 gpm. Over half of wells fall in the 5–15 gpm band, and another 34% are 15+ gpm.

Low producers do exist: about 3% of wells report under 1 gpm and 8% are in the 1–5 gpm range. For an exempt household well, even 1–2 gpm can work with proper storage, but it’s less forgiving if you plan irrigation. Before buying acreage in places like Wheat Ridge, Berkley or Twin Lakes, compare your target lot to the closest reported wells and pay attention to that small but real low-yield share.

sections.heading: Water levels and long-term trend
sections.html:
Static water levels near Mountain View are quite shallow. The median depth to water is about 13 feet, and the middle half of readings fall between 10 and 20 feet below ground. That shallow water table is one reason many wells don’t have to be drilled very deep.

Looking at measurements by decade, the median depth to water was about 15 feet in the 1950s, 18 feet in the 1960s, and then around 13 feet again in the 2010s and 2020s. That history doesn’t point to a steady long-term decline in this dataset. Still, local conditions can vary a lot block to block, so plan your pump setting with some margin below the static level, and keep an eye on new data if you’re planning a long-term home or larger landscaping demand.

sections.heading: Who’s drilling here and permit history
sections.html:
There’s a long record of well activity around Mountain View. The state shows 11,736 permits within about 5 miles, with 5,742 recorded as constructed and 6,425 reporting a total depth. Drilling really picked up in the 1990s and 2000s, with 2,223 permits in the 1990s and 2,298 in the 2000s, then 1,789 more in the 2010s. Another 874 permits have been issued in the 2020s so far, with records current through 2025.

Most wells are tagged as monitoring (about 55%), with domestic or household use making up roughly a quarter and some irrigation in the mix. That monitoring share reflects urban and industrial activity around Lakeside and North Washington. On the drilling side, Authorized (Pe, Pg), Layne, Christensen Co. (Tormoehlen, David A.), and Ground Exploration LLC (Bender, Joseph T.) are among the most active names in the records.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost here
sections.html:
Here the ground is Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, and typical drilling runs around $50–$70 per foot. With a local median depth of 29 feet, the drilled hole alone pencils out near $1,400–$2,000. By the time you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical, a finished residential well tends to land around $7,400–$14,000 based on that depth.

That range assumes you hit water at roughly the median depth. If your specific site ends up closer to the deeper end of what’s been drilled in this area, costs rise directly with every extra foot. When budgeting for a new build, I’d allow a margin above the median-based estimate until a driller has reviewed nearby well logs on and around your parcel.

sections.heading: Risks: contamination, low yield and construction limits
sections.html:
Beyond depth and yield, this area has some specific risks to check. Within about 10 miles, there are 660 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 89 historic mine features, and 187 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That doesn’t mean your well will be impacted, but it does mean water-quality testing should be non-negotiable before relying on a well long term.

On the supply side, a small share of wells do come in under 1 gpm or in the 1–5 gpm range, so dry or marginal holes are a real possibility on certain lots. With shallow water tables, you also need to site septic systems carefully to maintain separation from groundwater and wells. Have a local professional look at setbacks and space for both well and leach field before finalizing building plans.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot near Mountain View
sections.html:
If you’re eyeing land around Mountain View, Lakeside or Edgewater, start by pulling nearby well permits and noting depths, yields and uses. You’ve got a dense data set here: thousands of wells, mostly in the same Denver Basin setting, with a 29-foot median depth and 12.0 gpm median yield as a reference point.

For new construction, confirm that a domestic or household-use well permit is actually available for your parcel and that any subdivision covenants or water agreements are clear. In this part of Jefferson County, treat a full lab water test as part of your due diligence given the number of PFAS and cleanup sites in the wider area. Finally, coordinate well location early with driveway, foundation and septic layout so you don’t box yourself into a poor spot for one of those systems.

faq.q: How deep are water wells around Mountain View, Colorado?
faq.a: Within about 5 miles of Mountain View, the median well depth is 29 feet, and the middle half fall between 20 and 50 feet. Around 87% of recorded wells are shallower than 100 feet, while only about 3% go deeper than 600 feet. There are rare outliers, including one very deep well at 1,740 feet, but most homes in this area rely on relatively shallow completions in Denver Basin bedrock and local alluvium.

faq.q: How much water do Mountain View area wells usually produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields near Mountain View are generally strong. The median yield is 12.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half of wells between 8.0 and 15.0 gpm. About 55% of wells fall in the 5–15 gpm range and 34% are 15+ gpm. Only about 3% report under 1 gpm and 8% are in the 1–5 gpm band, so most household wells have more than enough capacity for typical indoor use and modest outdoor watering.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well near Mountain View, CO?
faq.a: In the Mountain View area, drilling through Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock typically runs about $50–$70 per foot. With a local median well depth of 29 feet, the drilled hole portion usually costs roughly $1,400–$2,000. A complete residential well system with casing, pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical commonly totals in the $7,400–$14,000 range at that depth. Deeper wells or difficult sites will increase the final cost proportionally.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink around Mountain View?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well. The area has 660 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 89 historic mine features, and 187 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those regional numbers mean groundwater quality can vary, even between nearby properties. Some wells may be perfectly fine while others show contaminants. Always plan on a comprehensive lab test for any existing or new well before using the water for drinking, and retest periodically.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping near Mountain View, Colorado?
faq.a: Available static water level data don’t show a clear long-term decline. The median depth to water was about 15 feet in the 1950s and 18 feet in the 1960s, then around 13 feet in both the 2010s and 2020s. Overall, the current median depth to water is about 13 feet, with most readings between 10 and 20 feet. That said, aquifer conditions can vary locally, so it’s still wise to design your well and pump with some reserve below the measured level.
